newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 23.

text.p: Prepared for The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- LABOUR PEER LORD HOLLICK MAKES 4.8 MILLIONS STG

The annual report from United News and Media says chief executive and Labour peer Lord Hollick has received 4.8 million stg from the company in the past 15 months. The group has also ended its donations to the Conservative Party. Charles Gregson, a director of the television and money-brokering business MAI, which merged with United last year, made two million stg.
-- BZW BONUS TARGET HIDDEN FROM AGM

Andrew Buxton, chairman of Barclays Bank, has been forced to defend pay policy at it's investment banking wing. Shareholders have approved a bonus scheme for more than 60 BZW executives without knowing what the targets were. For executives to get the bonuses, BZW will have to outperform performance thresholds, which will not be revealed until after the 1999 results are announced in 2000, for three-year rolling periods.
-- IMF CALL TO COOL UK ECONOMY WITH RISE IN INTEREST RATES

The International Monetary Fund is to call for a swift post-election rise in interest rates in Britain to prevent the economy from overheating. This will strengthen the hand of Eddie George, the governor of the Bank of England, when he meets with the chancellor on May 8. The support for higher rates will be part of an upbeat assessment of economic prospects. The IMF has raised its forecast for this year's growth from three percent to 3.3 percent, the fastest rate since 1994.
THE TIMES
-- TROUBLED M&G PLANS OVERHAUL OF STRATEGY

One of the UK's biggest fund managers, M&G, is planning to improve its poor investment performance with a complete overhaul of investment strategy. The company has come under increasing pressure from independent financial advisers, who provide M&G with half of its business, to tackle its performance problems. The advisors have become increasingly reluctant to advise clients to invest with the company.
-- CWS DIRECTOR CONFESSES TO HELPING REGAN BID

One of the directors suspended last week by the Co-operative Wholesale Society, Allan Green, has admitted he has been in secret meetings with Andrew Regan and David Lyons, the two men from Lanica Trust who set up Galileo to carry out a hostile bid for the society. Green admits he breached his authority and obligations. It has also emerged that Japanese bank Nomura is the chief backer of the bid, lending 1.2 billion stg to Galileo.
-- HALIFAX COULD FUEL ONE BILLION STG SPREE

The Halifax Building Society announced it will float on the stock market on June 2. Up to one billion stg could be ready for spending on June 7, even if only 10 percent of the 7.6 million beneficiaries opt to cash in their part of the 12 billion stg free share distribution at the earliest opportunity. Halifax said it had put a special mechanism in place to ensure that its customers did not suffer if there was a market setback during the first days as a quoted company.
THE GUARDIAN
-- NATWEST LOSSES REMAIN HIDDEN

A report by the team of accountants and lawyers looking into how NatWest lost 90 million stg on derivatives trading will be released next month. Bank chairman Lord Alexander said the full findings are unlikely to be made public for commercial and legal reasons. He called the loss a "setback" and said shareholders would be informed of any significant developments.
-- SMITHKLINE HIT BY STRONG POUND

Jan Leschley, chief executive of SmithKline Beecham, the drugs group, claims the soaring pound wiped more than 40 million stg off profits in the first three months of this year and that the impact could reach 100 million stg in the full year. SmithKline joins Unilever, Reed Elsevier, Glaxo Wellcome, ICI, British Steel and many others who have felt the effects of a strong pound.
-- SQUARE MILE GRIPPED IN FRENZY OF JOB HOPPING

A frenzy of headhunting and salary-hopping has gripped the Square Mile leading to nearly one-third of City stockbrokers and futures dealers to change jobs every year. Numbers have doubled since early 1990s, and anti-fraud regulators are being dragged into disputes between "defectors" and their former employers. City whizz-kids are being tempted with lavish contracts and bonus payments triggered by a Bank of England warning about the need to ensure bonus-chasing does not lead to risks that could destabilise big financial houses.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SCANDAL-RIDDEN NOMURA SAYS 'SAYONARA' TO ITS ENTIRE BOARD

Masashi Suzuki, president of the Japanese securities house Nomura, has resigned along with the 16-member board. This is the most dramatic and sweeping clearout ever by Japan's financial community. Suzuki said he had to accept responsibility for the racketeering scandal that has ruined Nomura's reputation. Hideo Sakamaki, former president of Nomura, testified that the firm had paid more than 70 million yen in stocks to accounts linked to racketeers.
-- LABOUR HOLDS NO FEARS FOR DFS

Graham Kirkham, owner of the DFS Furniture business and whose family is one of the biggest financial backers of the Conservative Party, said he will support the Labour Party. He believes his business would prosper no matter which government was in power. He said his senior management believed retailers prospered more under Labour governments.
-- ALLIANCE SHARES RETREAT BUT AUCTION PRICE RISES

The price of Alliance & Leicester shares have fallen 23.3 pence stg, but the average price paid in the second auction of unwanted shares rose to 551 pence. Broker to the share issue, Cazenove, said all 52.3 million shares in the second auction were sold. The results of a third auction will give the new bank an idea of whether any significant stakes have been accumulated, which could indicate the presence of a potential bidder.
